newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr idled by US$, near 6-yr high on mark.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr idled by US$, near 6-yr high on mark.

text.p: The Australian dollar drifted in becalmed seas Monday as the market contemplated yet another week of uncertainty over domestic interest rates.

Dealers say a 50 basis point cut in official rates to 5.0 percent has been largely priced in but other outcomes are possible and suspect the market will not know for sure until after the Reserve Bank's board meeting on August 5.

Although marooned on the US$, it sailed ahead on the mark -- to be a whisker away from six year highs -- and Swiss franc where investors were deserting in droves. But again volumes were light with prices being mainly marked up in line with the US$.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the dollar was idling at US$0.7380/85 from an early US$0.7374/79 after closing Friday at US$0.7404/09 having had a short covering bounce fail at US$0.7425 resistance.
The latter barrier was expected to cap the currency short term while support at US$0.7330 had proved a solid base last week and was not likely to be troubled today, said dealers.
The broader range of US$0.7310/7440 could well hold right up to the August 6 when the RBA's thinking on another easing, whether for or against, should become clearer.
If for, many felt the dollar could rally as long as the the easing was no more than the 50 basis points priced in.
If August 6 passed with no move, the market would begin to wonder if all the speculation had been in vain and the easing cycle actually ended with the last cut on May 23.
Such a development could see the dollar bounce sharply, although the RBA has caught the market by surprise enough times in the past to keep buyers cautious.
Data this week included the balance of goods and services, building approvals and retail trade but none should impact on rate expectations unless well outside forecasts.
The June trade balance on Tuesday should show the largest surplus ever but only thanks to accounting of the RBA gold sale.

The Bureau of Statistics plans to account for the RBA's sale of its gold reserves as exports and, since 125 tonnes of gold were sold forward for June delivery, analysts are expecting a surplus of anything up to A$2.2 billion.

That would be way up on May's A$873 million which itself was boosted by the sale of a A$500 million frigate and imply a hefty contribution to Q2 GDP from net exports. The effect of the gold sale on GDP would be largely negated however, as it implied a corresponding fall in stocks which would detract from GDP.
Building approvals for June are seen down 1.5 percent but that should not alter the outlook for a steady housing recovery.

The retail trade figures on Thursday could stir some market activity given how volatile the series has been in recent months. The median forecast is for a sober 0.4 percent rise in June following the steep 2.9 percent gain in May but estimates range from a rise of 1.5 percent to a fall of 1.5 percent.
Analysts felt it would take a rise of more than 2.0 percent to make the market reconsider its rate cut assumptions.

On the crosses the dollar extended gains on the mark to 1.3620/30 from 1.3582/04 and on the Swiss franc to 1.1215/20 from 1.1199/22. It firmed to 86.50/60 yen from 86.11/21 and to 57.7 in trade weighted terms from 57.6.-- Wayne Cole 9373 1800
